648.	Expenses in connection with Canada's participation in the world refugee year and, notwithstanding section 35 of the Financial Administration Act, to authorize payments to be made pursuant to this vote up to the 1st day of April, 1961; there shall be charged to this vote and included in the unexpended balance of vote 55 of the main estimates, 1959-60, an amount equal to the amount spent and charged to that vote in connection with the world refugee year, $600,000.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to recall to the committee that when we were discussing world refugee year in the last session of parliament I reminded hon. members that the government of Canada just before the Hungarian uprising had had a survey made by a senior officer of the immigration branch and a senior officer of the citizenship branch of the refugee camps in Europe with a view to seeing whether we could not on our own do something more than was then being done about reducing the population of these camps, and that by a curious coincidence I was on the verge of making certain recommendations to my colleagues when we were overwhelmed by the Hungarian problem and the matter was left in abeyance for the time being. I confess that I regret to have to say I never had another opportunity to make those recommendations.
Meanwhile, of course, the suggestion came for a general approach to this problem under the aegis of the United Nations commissioner for refugees in the form of world refugee year. We are all very pleased to hear the announcement the other day that the movement of the 100 families had been so successful and had cost so much less than was anticipated that the government proposed to make some extension of that program. When I have concluded perhaps the minister would tell us what numbers he envisages would be included in this extension. I am not going to urge at this time that there should be any very large increase in the strictly governmental participation in this scheme because I believe that the concrete and constructive suggestions I intend to make would in fact be preferable.
As soon as it was published I carefully examined the little booklet prepared by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration setting out the conditions for the admission of unsponsored and sponsored refugees to Canada. In most respects it seems to me these conditions are highly satisfactory. There is one of these conditions that has so far seemed to be an obstacle to one single refugee being brought to this country under private sponsorship. I should like to read that requirement to the committee. The requirement is that the sponsor must-and then

there are set out four requirements which I will not bother to read:
(v) provide assurance, where the refugee suffers from illness which will require treatment in Canada, that he will receive the medical care he needs. When the illness is such that institutional care is necessary, the approval of the provincial health authorities must be obtained before the refugee can be permitted to come to Canada.
The brochure then lists certain conditions that must be fulfilled by the refugee. He must be of good character and so forth.
It goes on to say:
The Canadian government does not set a limit to the period or to the extent of the responsibility assumed by the sponsors. Relief of indigent residents of Canada is normally the responsibility of the municipalities and the provinces. A sponsored immigrant who finds himself in need of assistance is a burden on the municipality or the province if his sponsor fails to live up to the guarantees he gave when applying for the immigrant's admission. This will explain that the Canadian government should insist that sponsors of immigrants, including refugees, accept full responsibility for the persons brought to Canada under their sponsorship until they become eligible for normal municipal or provincial social and welfare benefits. Sponsors who may wish to ascertain the extent of their responsibility and the nature of the welfare assistance available from municipal or provincial authorities, which vary from province to province, are requested to get in touch with these authorities for further information. Sponsors may also wish to take advantage of hospital insurance plans in respect of the refugees whom they have sponsored.
As the representations which were made to the Prime Minister the other day by the welfare council, and which the Prime Minister put on Hansard on March 3, clearly show, the welfare council and others interested have found that this requirement is one that is in fact in practice a bar to any effective action. It has proved to be up till now and in my opinion it will continue to be a complete bar. I know it is not intended to be. I am not for a minute suggesting that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration or the government as a whole put this requirement in deliberately to make the sponsorship unworkable, but that has been the effect of it.
Not only has it been the effect, but it is precisely what I told the Secretary of State for External Affairs in the last session of parliament would be the effect. I had some experience in administering the Hungarian refugee movement and I know that it is almost impossible for the federal government to negotiate with provincial and municipal authorities about this particular matter with any finality or with any satisfaction, and it is quite impossible for private sponsors to do it. I am sure that is why the welfare council made the recommendation it did. It was that the federal government, in consultation with the provinces, arrange as expeditiously as possible for the acceptance of
Supply-External Affairs public responsibility for established public health and welfare services for privately sponsored refugee families admitted under the government's program for private sponsorship during the world refugee year.
When the Prime Minister announced on the seventeenth of March the decisions that the government had already reached with respect to these representations he said that they had agreed with some of them, and I am sure that there was a good deal of satisfaction taken over that. The first of their recommendations and, far and away, sir, the most important of them, the Prime Minister said he was not able to deal with at that time because a decision had not been reached about it. Now, here is my suggestion. I do not agree entirely with the recommendation of the welfare council and I am going beyond what they suggested. If we really mean business at all about this world refugee year and about private sponsorship-personally I should like to see more private sponsorship and that is what I am urging, more private sponsorship and more ease for private sponsorship instead of any large addition to the direct government movement-I am quite convinced that this problem can be very easily solved if the government will do, with respect to these privately sponsored refugees, precisely what was done in the case of the Hungarian refugees.
The federal government should undertake the residual responsibility of health care after a certain period for those refugees who are admitted and who are going to be selected by the United Nations commissioner for refugees. I think it is quite reasonable to expect that the sponsors should look after them for a year. It seems to me, sir, that should be done instead of trying to leave the sponsors with an open-ended commitment which many of those voluntary organizations cannot in conscience undertake because they cannot be sure that two years hence they may have the same officers or the same personnel or, in fact, that they will be in a position to carry it out. Most of them are composed of people who take their responsibilities and regard their word seriously, and would not want to subscribe their names to something that was not going to be carried out.
It seems to me, sir, that this is not suggesting any very great burden on the treasury. I am going to give two reasons for this view. The first is the one that was given the other day by the Prime Minister or by the Secretary of State for External Affairs; I forget which one of them it was that told us how much less costly and how much more encouraging this movement of the 100 families was than it was expected to be,

Supply-External Affairs how much more quickly those people were recovering and how much easier the integration was proving to be. But I think even more striking, sir, were the answers which the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration gave the other day to the questions I put on the order paper about the Hungarian refugee movement.
As the committee knows, we admitted to this country 37,727 Hungarian refugees, most of them without any medical examination whatsoever before they arrived in Canada. It is true they were given a medical examination for the purpose of determining after they got here whether they could be landed as immigrants or whether they would be admitted temporarily under other status. Now, it happens that 1,380 of those 37,000 were allowed entry as non-immigrants and, in most cases, they were allowed entry as non-immigrants for health reasons because they could not satisfy the medical requirements. Three years later there are only 17 of those people receiving help from the federal government out of a total of 37,700. Out of 1,380 who could not satisfy health requirements-I do not say they were all people who could not satisfy the health requirements 'but most of them would have been-there are 17 today, three years later, receiving help from the federal government.
If I may be permitted, sir, to refer to this, the other day I had the privilege of attending the tea given by the Hungarian-Canadian committee in Knox church, and I wish that every hon. member could have been there because that function was organized almost entirely not by the older Hungarian community, though they helped, but by people who came here three years ago without a thing except the clothes they were wearing and who today are as well dressed as anybody you would see in Ottawa. Most of them spoke very good English, and it was a function that anyone in any part of Canada would have been proud to have had a part in organizing. Now, sir, that was something that was possible because the Hungarian refugees did not moulder away for years in camps. There was enough action taken, enough co-operation and enough world interest to get them dealt with quickly. We can hardly expect quite as good results in the case of the residual population of those camps who have been there for so long; but surely that is all the more reason why we should do everything practicable that we can to make a really worth-while contribution to this refugee problem.
I do believe that there is plenty of voluntary enthusiasm for this refugee movement of a practical nature and that if we could get

rid of this one obstacle with regard to continuing health care-I do not say that the government should do it all; I think it would be quite reasonable to say that the sponsors should take that responsibility for the first year but I feel that the government can do what we did for the Hungarians-then after one year if the refugees cannot satisfy the normal municipal or provincial health and welfare requirements for such care as is ^publicly given by these provinces or municipalities, the federal government should in fact accept that residual responsibility. If that were done I venture to say that on that basis it would cost a very small sum indeed. It would remove the most irritating obstacle, and it is really not reasonable to expect the municipal and provincial governments to give commitments about this matter. I am sure that the Minister of Labour, who was once the mayor of one of the leading cities in Ontario, would agree, because I know he held those views some years ago when I was minister of immigration and he was a private member of this house. These people may live in a municipality and then go somewhere else, or they may not ever have been taxpayers of the municipality at all. There is migration from one province to another.
As a matter of fact, what we are trying to do here is to make a national contribution to this problem. All of us with experience know this will continue to be a practical obstacle to the movement of people, and it could be removed for a very small contribution. It does seem to me, sir, that it should and could be done and that the vast majority of the Canadian people would be very pleased indeed to see their government do it. I am sorry the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration are not here to listen to what I have to say. I am sure that with the experience they have had already they would find it very difficult to disagree with the opinion I have expressed.
I know from my experience that in the final analysis the barrier that has to be overcome is the barrier provided by the treasury board and its chairman. The chairman of the treasury board is in front of me, and I appeal to his large heart, as well as to his head, because I venture to say, sir, that most of these people who may require medical care now will be making a contribution five years from now to the production of this country out of all proportion to anything it will cost the taxpayers to carry out the suggestion I have made.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister for some clarification of this particular item. Last year the Minister of Agriculture told us that we had a surplus of about 25 million pounds of skimmed milk that we could not give away. Yet we have found that in one year we have been able to give away $1 million worth of skimmed milk powder.

This assistance covers subsidies on dragger and long-liner vessels and was first introduced during the war. My reason for insisting on this is that the fisherman who purchases a boat that costs him $70,000 is put to very heavy expense which he has to cover during the fishing period which in most of the provinces, especially in New Brunswick, Quebec and Prince Edward Island, is limited to a season of six months.
On a $70,000 boat the fisherman is called upon to pay at least $2,000 a year in interest alone. He has to pay insurance costs in the vicinity of $1,000 besides that. In most cases he has to pay municipal taxes on the vessel amounting to $700 or often up to $1,000 a year.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to support this vote. I should like to say a word about the incumbent with whom I have been associated for a period of many years, first in my capacity as a member of parliament for the constituency of Stormont, from which he came, and that of Glengarry as well, but more importantly in my capacity as an honorary colonel of the Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry Highlanders. Colonel Franklin and myself share that honour and that distinction. I feel that on this vote I should express a word of appreciation, I am sure on behalf of those who sit on this side of the house, for his excellent services during the many years he acted as Sergeant-at-Arms.
He was not only a soldier of repute but also proved in this difficult position to be a good administrator. He was above all, I think, a fine gentleman. Colonel Franklin's record in two world wars is one which I am sure most of us here know. His record in the first world war was one of distinction. In the second world war, he immediately offered to mobilize the first battalion of the Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry Highlanders, and that he did with immediate success, but afterwards took command of the second battalion. It was during the period of time that I was on the other side of the chamber and was minister of transport that he was appointed to the position he held with such distinction and, I believe, with such satisfaction to all sides of the House of Commons during his time in office.
I should particularly like to refer to his ability to get along with not only the members of the House of Commons but the many people on the staff who are obliged to come in contact with the Sergeant-at-Arms repeatedly. I think I can safely say that this statement applied to him not only during the years up to June, 1957, but afterwards. It was a position that required a great deal of tact and Colonel Franklin was known for that characteristic.
I think the government should be commended for introducing this item in the estimates. I am positive it will be supported not only by us but by all members who sit on both sides of the chamber who, I trust, will find it possible to approve the words which I have just expressed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I thank the hon. gentleman for what he has said. For my part I should like to join very heartily in the tribute he paid to Colonel Franklin. I had a very happy and warm personal

Supply-Legislation
relationship with Colonel Franklin. In the 15 years we had been together here I think the friendship which I had been privileged to enjoy with Colonel Franklin was probably unusually warm. I can most heartily and sincerely endorse what the hon. member for Laurier has said about Colonel Franklin.
Just recently I had occasion to convey to Colonel Franklin an expression of personal regard and esteem for the long public service he has rendered. He was a man of very great tact and indeed a man of considerable personal charm. One could not ask for anything happier than the way in which Colonel Franklin addressed himself to the wide variety of duties that fall upon the shoulders of the Sergeant-at-Arms. A great deal of versatility is required of the incumbent of that position. Colonel Franklin's service to the Canadian people through this parliament I am sure will be long and gratefully remembered.
I think we may all be happy indeed at the thought that now in his retirement he is enjoying good health, and we hope he may look forward to many years of happiness in his retirement and the well-earned leisure that goes with it. I appreciate indeed what the hon. gentleman has said about the provision that has been made for his benefit by this item. I hope it will commend itself to all hon. members.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have other opportunities and means of expressing my appreciation of Lieutenant Colonel Franklin, retired Sergeant-at-Arms, but I should not like the opportunity to pass, as I am now in my seat when this vote is before the committee, without saying that I endorse what has been said by the hon. member for Laurier and the Minister of Finance, particularly as I had the responsibility of working with Colonel Franklin, when he was Sergeant-at-Arms, more closely perhaps than other hon. members of the house. In the three years in which I have occupied the chair I have enjoyed that association and have found him at all times to be a co-operative, and able officer of good judgment. I wholeheartedly endorse what has been said and add my best wishes to Colonel Franklin in his retirement.

On behalf of this group I want to express their appreciation of the services rendered by Colonel Franklin over a good number of years and to wish him a lengthy, happy and healthy retirement. Having said that, I should like to ask the minister why this item is necessary. Would the minister mind explaining this item? It is not quite clear to some of the members of this group.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Very simply the explanation is this. Colonel Franklin had not completed in the prescribed time the papers that were necessary in order to enjoy the benefit of file supplementary death benefit plan under the superannuation act.

I want to express my appreciation to the Minister of Finance for the words he has uttered under this item today about the former Sergeant-at-Arms and to concur with the remarks made by him, by the Speaker of the house and by the hon. member for Laurier. I greatly doubt whether too many hon. members appreciate fully the amount of detail and work involved each time there is a change of parliament. Such a change creates problems requiring infinite judgment, care and patience. I think Colonel Franklin showed great fairness of mind in those many small but intensely practical problems that arise each time parliament changes, and there have been several of those changes since 1945. Holding that view, I was most appreciative of the remarks of the Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Laurier, His Honour the Speaker of the house and the hon. member for Kootenay West.
There is one point I want to mention about this item. I think it should be mentioned but I do not want my remarks to be misunderstood. I hold the view that the method of the termination of the appointment left something to be desired. We were dealing with an officer of parliament and the officer of parliament concerned is appointed by letters patent-in other words, a commission -almost identical in form with those under which a minister of the crown is appointed.
There is, of course, no question at all as to the right to terminate that appointment at any time. However, I thought that the method of termination without notice on this occasion surely left something to be desired, bearing in mind the fact that the government was dealing with an officer of parliament. I do not want to elaborate unduly on the subject but surely when dealing with an officer of parliament, and particularly one with such an outstanding record, he having also served outside of parliament with such distinction in one of the fine historic regiments of Canada, a little bit more care and a somewhat better technique could have been used in carrying out the termination of the appointment. I do not wish to pursue the matter unduly. However, I should like to feel that the government would take note of my remarks and that, if the occasion ever arises in the future to deal with a similar matter, more care would be used.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON AIR DEFENCE PROGRAM
speechtext: I should like to ask the house for unanimous consent to revert to motions so that I may make a further statement regarding the air defence plan.

speechtext: Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON AIR DEFENCE PROGRAM
speechtext:
I should like to make a further statement in amplification of the replies I made in the house this morning regarding the revision of the air defence program. As I mentioned this morning, the United States air force has put certain proposals before the appropriations committee of the house of representatives. The United States authorities are releasing at this hour the gist of their proposals which were made to the house of representatives subcommittee yesterday, and I feel it appropriate that this house should be informed of these changes. I should add that this is the statement which is being released by the United States defence department at this time:
The United States air force has proposed substantial changes in its air defence and strategic programs to expedite missile detection systems, to bring in a simplified air defence system at an earlier date, and increase ICBM capability.
The proposal recommends that these projects be financed primarily with funds which would be made available by a reduction in the Bomarc "B" production program and cancellation of the planned installation of advanced SAGE combat centres. An effective SAGE system for control of Bomarc and interceptors will be completed.
The projects recommended by the Air Force include:
1.	The acceleration of MIDAS, the satellite system designed to detect ICBMs at the earliest possible moment after launch.
2.	The acceleration of the second and third units of the ballistic missile early warning system, the first of whose powerful radars is scheduled to become operational within the next few months.
3.	Improvement of the capability of "Century Series" interceptors and modernization of current radar coverage.
Air Defence Program
4.	Technical development of an advanced fire control and missile system for interceptors.
5.	An increase in the number of Atlas intercontinental ballistic missiles previously programmed to be on launch pads in calendar year 1962. This would be accomplished by increasing the number of missiles and launch pads of some Atlas squadrons previously announced.
6.	Insurance of expeditious development and reliability testing of "minuteman," the solid fuel ICBM which is to be manufactured in quantities for installation in hardened underground sites and on railway cars moving at random about the country.
The completed air defence system proposed under the change in program would be operational at least two years earlier than the system previously planned.
These changes will contribute generally to an earlier and effective practical air defence against the weapons on which the Soviet will have to rely for decisive attack within the next several years.
The recommended projects would cost in the order of $500 million during fiscal years 1960 and 1961. The proposed reduction of Bomarc B production and elimination of the hardened SAGE combat centres would make available funds to finance the recommended projects.
The proposed transfer of funds was submitted in classified detail to the house appropriations committee in executive session on March 24, 1960.
The program changes were proposed on the grounds that emphasis in the over-all threat is shifting towards ballistic missiles and that several years' time would be required to bring the advance SAGE combat centres in hardened sites to full operational status. SAGE stands for semi-automatic ground environment. It is an electronic air warning and air defence weapons control network, the heart of which is a computer built by the military products division of International Business Machines at Kingston, New York.
SAGE installations which can be in operation much earlier than those previously proposed in the hardened supercombat centres are scheduled to be completed.
The Bomarc is a surface to air missile developed by the Boeing Airplane Company to operate with all other air defence weapons under direction of the SAGE system. Under the proposed shift in funds, Bomarc units in the revised program would be concentrated in the industrial northeast.
The proposed reduction in total Bomarc strength will not affect Bomarc squadrons programmed for the Royal Canadian Air Force.
Included in the revised air defence budget are provisions for SAGE direction and control in Canada. The Canadian Minister of National Defence has been kept fully informed throughout development of the air force's modified air defence plan.
In further explanation I might say this means that instead of the advanced SAGE combat centre which I announced in July last year it is now propsed to install in Canada a tube SAGE combat centre in lieu of the previously planned transistorized centre. While this program forecasts a reduction in the number of Bomarc B's to be produced in the United States, this reduction does not interfere with the two Bomarc installations which are to be located in Canada. It is still the intention that there will be two Canadian Bomarc sites as an integral part of the modified Bomarc system.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON AIR DEFENCE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister's statement is obviously a very important one on a vitally important subject. It would not be the part of responsibility on our side to comment on it in any final way until we have had a chance to examine its implications for continental defence and for Canada. I have not yet had that opportunity. The minister with his usual courtesy and consideration in these matters indicated that he would try to give me a copy in advance but it was not possible to do that-and I do not criticize him for this-until I was just entering the house. Therefore, I have not had sufficient opportunity to examine this statement which is such an important and complicated one.
From reading the statement and listening to the minister, however, it is quite clear in my mind that it represents what perhaps may be called a major shift in United States defence policy although apparently not such a shift in that part of the continental defence policy which has been allocated to Canada. It seems clear from this statement that in Washington there is now going to be greater emphasis on the deterrent and less emphasis on defence as such in the hope, no doubt, that by a more effective and powerful deterrent there will be no need for strict defence because it will prevent attack.
This emphasis on the deterrent seems to be shown not only by the reduction in the support to be given by the United States government to Bomarc and to the semi-automatic ground environmental system, but also by the information contained in this statement that there is to be an increase in the resources to be allocated to intercontinental ballistic missiles and to the ballistic missile early warning system.
That in my view, if I understand it correctly, represents a very important shift in United States defence policy which is bound, of course, to have an effect on Canada. But the effect in terms of immediate policy does not seem to be shown in this statement because, as I understand it, while the United States government is abandoning to a very large extent Bomarc and SAGE, restricting Bomarc to the defence of the northeast according to the statement, the two Canadian Bomarc squadrons and the SAGE installations in support of those squadrons are to be maintained. In other words, this statement would appear to indicate that the minister's confidence in this particular weapon remains unimpaired. Perhaps I might put it this way: The United States has changed the kite but the tail remains the same.

subtopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON AIR DEFENCE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the most significant things in the
[Mr. Pearkes.l
minister's statement is the further confirmation of the very inferior role that Canada is playing in the so-called defence partnership with the United States. As I see our position, there is no longer, if indeed there ever was, a real partnership. The minister in his statement pointed out that the proposed transfer of funds was submitted in classified detail to the house appropriations committee in executive session on March 24, 1960. In other words, this is strictly a made-in-Washington policy in which Canada has had no effective voice.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON AIR DEFENCE PROGRAM
speechtext: That is not correct, of course.

subtopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON AIR DEFENCE PROGRAM
speechtext:
The change in United States emphasis away from the Bomarc to intercontinental ballistic missiles demonstrates that the military minds in the United States have decided for all practical purposes that the Bomarc is an ineffective weapon and is in fact a dead duck but Canada remains committed to what is obviously a useless military expenditure in terms of defence, something we in this group have been saying for a long time.
We think every great military authority will confirm that Bomarc weapons are unable to prevent bombers coming through that might be attacking this continent. Even if the Bomarc were operative sufficient planes would get through at any time to destroy the North American continent. We are opposed to the procedure in this regard because we are opposed to nuclear weapons on Canadian soil and in the future these weapons will be equipped with nuclear warheads.
We feel there is altogether too much money being spent on armaments at this time. Those armaments are already obsolete. The minister's statement indicates that we are correct in our view. There should be a large cut in military expenditures and a transfer of this money to economic assistance and improvements in the living standards in underdeveloped countries. This is an indication that on this continent the departments of defence of both Canada and the United States are out of step with the thinking of the people of the world. Now is the time for agreement on disarmament and a change in emphasis from military expenditures to peace expenditures. There is much evidence to support this view.

Would the house leader not consider putting over the federal-provincial tax-sharing resolution until Friday, say, because of the fact that many of us who would like to participate in this matter are also on the railways and shipping committee which, as the minister knows, will be sitting on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday of next week.

speechtext: We will make some such arrangement. I was wondering whether, if the resolution passed without further debate on Wednesday, we could have the bill in front of us for full debate on Friday. If, on the other hand, that does not suit, we might discuss it on Monday.
